Evidence Readings/Same year, different number
Evidence Reading

Same year, different number

Successive annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden give very different remittance values for 2024. A revision of this size is a measurement event to be explained before it can be read as an economic story.

Evidence period
Reference years 2021–2024 · CBY-Aden annual reports 2024 and 2025 · IMF Article IV consultation 2025
Last reviewed
26 September 2026

Do not infer: No single series is the correct level; no single scale factor — such as the roughly constant ratio of 1.838 between the CBY-Aden and IMF remittance series, or the 33% population share the IMF used for areas administered from Aden — is a universal conversion; net errors and omissions are not hidden remittances; and a residual-model estimate is not a baseline.

Two annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) give markedly different remittance values for the same reference year. The 2024 report put remittances in 2024 at USD 6.245 billion; the 2025 report restated 2024 at about USD 3.42 billion.

The gap is large, but the first thing it establishes is not that remittances collapsed. Both values describe 2024. Before the difference can be read as economic movement, the change in statistical vintage, scope or method has to be understood.

Same year, two published values

Analytical text alternative
  1. Analytical question: How should the same reference year be read across publication vintages?
  2. What the evidence shows: The 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) published remittances of US$6,245 million for 2024; the 2025 annual report restated 2024 at US$3,422.16 million. This is a restatement of the same year, not a fall between years. Indexed to 2021 = 100, the CBY-Aden 2025-report path and the IMF 2025 Article IV staff-report path both reach about 118 in 2024. The two indexed paths are almost identical: the annual-growth gap over 2022–2024 is at most about 0.0032 percentage points, and the CBY-Aden level stays about 1.838 times the IMF level over 2021–2024. They cannot be read as two independent confirmations of the trend, and their raw levels are not equivalent.
  3. Scope and time: Reference year 2024 in two publication vintages; indexed paths 2021–2024 · Remittances as defined by each source: annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for 2024 and 2025; IMF 2025 Article IV staff report, on the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government
  4. What not to conclude: A same-year restatement is not a fall between years. The raw levels of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) and IMF series are not equivalent, and their near-identical indexed paths cannot be read as two independent confirmations of the trend.
Reference year 2024 in two publication vintages; indexed paths 2021–2024Remittances as defined by each source: annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) for 2024 and 2025; IMF 2025 Article IV staff report, on the IMF's analytical scope for areas under the internationally recognized government

Two publications, one reference year

Revisions are normal in economic statistics. They become consequential when the revised value is large enough to change the baseline that analysis depends on, and this one is.

So “2024 remittances” is not precise enough on its own when two official publications attach materially different values to that year. The publication vintage has to travel with the reference year.

The shape of the series is a clue, not a crosswalk

When the remittance series in the 2025 CBY-Aden report and the IMF’s 2025 Article IV series are each indexed to 2021 = 100, their paths through 2024 are almost identical: the largest difference in annual growth over 2022–2024 is 0.0032 percentage points. Their levels are not: in every year from 2021 to 2024 the CBY-Aden value is 1.838 times the IMF value.

That regularity is useful. It suggests closely related trajectories compiled under different scopes or methods. It does not supply a conversion formula, and nothing public explains what the ratio represents.

IMF documentation describes a reconstruction of Yemen’s external-sector statistics under severe data constraints, including a model of personal transfers where information on informal channels was limited. That is method context. It does not reveal the exact formula behind each value in the CBY-Aden annual report.

A statistical clue is not yet a documented crosswalk.

Why the revision matters

Remittances matter at several levels at once: household livelihoods, the supply of foreign exchange, balance-of-payments analysis and the channels, formal and informal, through which money moves. A large revision to the macro series can therefore shift several analytical baselines without any new event in a single household.

Read without both the reference year and the publication vintage, a statistical revision can be mistaken for growth or collapse. Read with both, the useful question becomes: what changed in the measurement, and what, if anything, changed in the economy?

What this evidence does not tell us

It does not show that one series is correct for every purpose and the other wrong, and it offers no general conversion factor between the CBY-Aden and IMF series. It says nothing about how remittances are distributed across households, governorates or channels. And net errors and omissions in the balance of payments cannot be relabelled as unrecorded remittances: the residual balances the accounts; it is not an observed flow.

How to use the figures

For trend analysis, use a consistent statistical vintage wherever possible, and where the vintage changes, show the break. For scenario work it is legitimate to keep more than one baseline, provided each result says which one it uses. In public communication, describe a same-year difference as a statistical restatement, not as movement from one year to the next.

What would change this reading?

A primary methodological note linking the restated CBY-Aden series to the external-sector reconstruction would change the analysis materially. The most useful note would set out the scope, the source inputs, the treatment of informal flows, the revision policy and how the old and new vintages relate.

Until it exists, keep the vintage with the number.
